# **Unified Deep Learning Solution for Signal-Degraded Image Restoration and Super-Resolution under Hardware Constraints**

## **Architectural Design of Unified Denoising and Super-Resolution Networks**

### **Structural Analysis of Modern Image Restoration Models**

Restoring signal-degraded images in precision measurement and inspection systems requires architectures capable of simultaneously reversing spatial downsampling and removing severe noise corruption1. Image degradation in high-precision domains involves complex interactions between spatial information loss (downsampling from ![][image1] to ![][image2], or ![][image2] to ![][image3]), additive Gaussian noise, and multiplicative speckle noise2. Traditional single-task models designed strictly for super-resolution often amplify underlying noise, whereas dedicated denoising models tend to smooth away critical high-frequency edge detail required for dimensional measurement4.  
Deep learning architectures for image restoration have evolved from classical multi-stage Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to Vision Transformers (ViTs) and U-shaped encoder-decoder networks1. While Transformer-based backends achieve strong representation capabilities through self-attention mechanisms6, their quadratic computational complexity with respect to spatial token length introduces memory bottlenecks and execution latencies1. In high-throughput industrial and laboratory inspection scenarios evaluated on enterprise accelerators like the NVIDIA H100 GPU, total runtime encompasses model initialization, disk read/write cycles, and tensor execution. Consequently, heavy Transformer backbones often incur runtime penalties that outweigh their incremental quality gains1.  
U-shaped architectures featuring skip connections remain the foundational paradigm for low-level visual restoration1. Skip connections preserve fine spatial gradients across multi-scale feature maps, enabling the network to reconstruct high-resolution edge boundaries while filtering out stochastic noise at deeper semantic layers1.

### **Nonlinear Activation-Free Network Design for High-Throughput Inference**

To achieve high metric scores in Structural Similarity (SSIM), Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), and Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS) while minimizing inference latency, the Nonlinear Activation-Free Network (NAFNet) provides an efficient structural baseline11. NAFNet systematically simplifies traditional restoration blocks by eliminating standard nonlinear activation functions, including Rectified Linear Units (ReLU), Gaussian Error Linear Units (GELU), and Sigmoid functions11.  
In standard deep networks, activation functions introduce computational overhead and memory traffic due to elementwise transcendental operations1. NAFNet demonstrates that explicit nonlinear activations can be replaced by gating mechanisms and simplified channel transformations without degrading feature expressiveness11. The core NAFNet block replaces conventional activation layers with the SimpleGate module1. For an input feature map ![][image4], the channels are split into two equal partitions ![][image5], and their elementwise product is computed:  
![][image6]  
This gating operation mimics the behavior of gated activations such as ![][image7] while reducing floating-point operations (FLOPs) and memory access cost1. Furthermore, NAFNet replaces conventional Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) channel attention with Simplified Channel Attention (SCA)1. Standard attention modules utilize multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) with non-linear activation functions and Sigmoid boundaries to compute channel weights12. SCA simplifies this to a spatial global average pooling followed by a single linear convolution step without sigmoid bounds:  
![][image8]  
where ![][image9] represents a ![][image10] convolutional operator12. Omitting the Sigmoid function allows the network to assign negative weights or scaling factors greater than unity, expanding dynamic feature calibration12.  
To maintain training stability and preserve feature magnitude across deep architectures, Batch Normalization is replaced by Layer Normalization (![][image11])11. Batch Normalization suffers from high variance when processing small batch sizes during high-resolution restoration11. Layer Normalization operates independently across spatial dimensions per sample, stabilizing variance and preventing gradient explosion during multi-task degradation learning12.

| **NAFNet Baseline** | 17.1 | 40.30 | 33.69 | Baseline (![][image12]) | SimpleGate \+ Simplified Channel Attention \+ LayerNorm11 |
| **Restormer** | 26.1 | 40.02 | 32.92 | ![][image13] | Transposed Multi-Head Self-Attention \+ Gated Feed-Forward7 |

### **Upsampling Mechanisms for Spatial Resolution Restoration**

Restoring spatial resolution from degraded low-resolution inputs (![][image17] or ![][image18]) requires embedding efficient spatial upsampling operators directly into the network pipeline13. Three upsampling methods are evaluated: transposed convolution (deconvolution), bilinear/bicubic interpolation followed by convolution, and sub-pixel convolution (PixelShuffle).  
Transposed convolutions introduce checkerboard artifacts caused by overlapping kernel weights during stride calculations. Interpolation followed by standard convolution avoids checkerboards but incurs extra memory bandwidth overhead by performing feature extraction on high-resolution spatial dimensions8. Sub-pixel convolution performs feature extraction entirely within the lower-resolution spatial domain and redistributes channel dimensions into spatial dimensions at the final layer13.  
Given an upsampling factor ![][image19] and an intermediate feature map ![][image20], the PixelShuffle operator rearranges elements to yield an output tensor ![][image21]. Executing the core encoding, bottleneck, and decoding stages at the input resolution (![][image22]) minimizes memory bandwidth consumption on the H100 GPU8, restricting spatial upscaling strictly to the final layer.

## **Mathematical Degradation Modeling and Signal Pre-processing Strategies**

### **Physics of Multiplicative Speckle Noise and Intensity Out-of-Bounds Handling**

Precision inspection images acquired through coherent illumination, laser scanners, or acoustic imaging exhibit severe speckle noise alongside additive thermal noise and spatial downsampling. Unlike additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN), speckle noise is inherently signal-dependent and multiplicative:  
![][image23]  
where ![][image24] is the ground-truth high-resolution image normalized to ![][image25], ![][image26] represents spatial downsampling by factor ![][image27], ![][image28] is gamma-distributed or Rayleigh-distributed multiplicative speckle noise with unit mean ![][image29], and ![][image30] is additive thermal noise2.  
Because ![][image28] takes values strictly greater than ![][image31], the product ![][image32] expands the local pixel intensity range beyond the nominal ![][image25] ground-truth bounds. Histogram analysis of degraded images reveals long right-side tails, where pixel intensities reach values such as ![][image33] or higher. Naively clipping input pixel intensities to ![][image25] prior to network processing destroys high-frequency structural information encoded within bright intensity peaks, causing permanent information loss.  
In the proposed pipeline, raw degraded images are ingested as unclipped 32-bit floating-point tensors (float32). This maintains the full intensity distribution throughout feature extraction, allowing convolutional filters to leverage the complete dynamic range before bounding output predictions.

### **Variance Stabilizing Transformations and Normalization Pipelines**

To mitigate the signal-dependent variance of multiplicative noise, mathematical transformations are applied during data loading3. The Generalized Anscombe Transform converts signal-dependent Poisson-speckle processes into an approximate Gaussian distribution with stabilized unit variance3. For pure multiplicative noise, the logarithmic variance stabilizing transformation converts the product into an additive domain:  
![][image34]  
where ![][image35] is a small scalar preventing logarithmic singularity at zero intensity. Operating in the logarithmic domain converts heavy-tailed multiplicative distributions into symmetric, additive quasi-Gaussian distributions, matching the mathematical assumptions of standard convolutional filters2.  
Alternatively, direct unclipped float32 standard tensor normalization preserves raw physical intensities:  
![][image36]  
where mean ![][image37] and standard deviation ![][image38] are calculated over the raw, unclipped training distribution. This preserves linear dynamic range and enables the network to process values outside ![][image25].

### **Post-Processing and Dynamic Range Calibration**

While input processing preserves out-of-bounds intensity values to facilitate feature extraction, final output predictions must map back to the ground-truth intensity range ![][image25] to optimize PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS metrics.  
Direct hard clamping (![][image39]) at the network output layer introduces sharp gradient discontinuities during training and creates flat saturation regions in bright structures. To address this, a smooth parametric Soft-Clipping operator is integrated at the output stage:  
![][image40]  
This soft boundary function maintains continuous, non-zero backpropagation gradients for predictions slightly exceeding ![][image31], smoothly guiding spatial intensities back into the ground-truth interval ![][image25] during training epochs.

## **Multi-Objective Loss Function Engineering for Benchmarked Metrics**

### **Distortion Metric Optimization: PSNR and Structural Fidelity**

Evaluation relies on three distinct metrics: Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), Structural Similarity Index Metric (SSIM), and Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS)17. Optimizing for these metrics presents conflicting objective constraints19.  
PSNR is inversely proportional to Mean Squared Error (![][image41]):  
![][image42]  
Directly minimizing ![][image43] loss maximizes PSNR but causes over-smoothing and blurry edge reconstructions4. The network produces pixelwise averages across probable high-frequency spatial configurations, penalizing fine texture restoration4. To overcome this, the Charbonnier Loss (a smooth variant of ![][image44] loss) is selected as the primary pixel-level distortion objective20:  
![][image45]  
where ![][image46] provides numerical stability near zero gradients. Charbonnier loss penalizes small pixel errors less severely than ![][image43] while applying stronger gradients to larger edge mismatches, preserving structural sharpness4.  
To optimize SSIM directly, a differentiable Multi-Scale Structural Similarity (![][image47]) loss is added4:  
![][image48]  
where ![][image49], ![][image50], and ![][image51] evaluate luminance, contrast, and structural comparison at ![][image52] downsampled scale spaces18. MS-SSIM enforces structural preservation across spatial frequencies, penalizing halo artifacts introduced by deblurring filters4.

### **Perceptual Detail Reconstruction: Deep Feature Loss Integration**

While Charbonnier and MS-SSIM losses drive pixel-level fidelity (PSNR and SSIM), they do not maximize LPIPS scores4. LPIPS evaluates deep feature representations extracted from pre-trained networks (e.g., VGG-16 or AlexNet) across intermediate activation layers4:  
![][image53]  
where ![][image54] represents normalized feature activations at layer ![][image55], and ![][image56] denotes learned scaling weights4. Minimizing ![][image57] forces the network to reconstruct high-frequency visual textures matching the perceptual distribution of clean images4.  
To preserve edge boundaries without introducing non-differentiable overhead during inference, a Spatial Gradient Loss (![][image58]) is integrated to penalize high-frequency edge degradation5:  
![][image59]  
where ![][image60] and ![][image61] represent Sobel edge operators.

### **Multi-Objective Optimization and Dynamic Loss Weighting**

Combining pixel distortion, structural similarity, and perceptual losses into a single scalar objective requires precise loss weight balancing4:  
![][image62]  
Unweighted combinations often suffer from gradient dominance, where perceptual gradients (![][image57]) overwhelm pixel-level fidelity gradients (![][image63]), leading to high LPIPS scores but severe PSNR degradation4. To optimize across all three target metrics, Multi-Objective Optimization (MOO) dynamically scales loss coefficients based on homoscedastic task uncertainty or gradient norm balancing (GradNorm)19.

| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Charbonnier Loss** | PSNR | ![][image64] | ![][image31] | Ensures pixelwise color/intensity alignment4 |
| **MS-SSIM Loss** | SSIM | ![][image65] | ![][image66] | Preserves multi-scale contrast and structural bounds4 |
| **LPIPS (VGG Feature)** | LPIPS | ![][image67] | ![][image68] | Reconstructs realistic high-frequency micro-textures4 |
| **Sobel Gradient Loss** | SSIM / PSNR | ![][image69] | ![][image70] | Sharpen edge transitions and suppress noise blur5 |

## **High-Performance Hardware Acceleration on NVIDIA H100 Architectures**

### **Graph Compilation and Kernel Fusion via PyTorch Inductor**

Evaluating models on NVIDIA H100 GPUs requires optimizing execution speeds to minimize overall benchmark runtime8. PyTorch 2.x torch.compile accelerates deep learning inference by compiling Python network definitions into fused C++/Triton GPU kernels using the Inductor backend8.  
In standard eager execution, each operator (e.g., LayerNorm, SimpleGate, Conv2D) triggers an independent CUDA kernel launch, creating significant CPU-side launch overhead. Compiled execution fuses contiguous elementwise operators into single Triton kernel launches, reducing memory access round-trips to GPU High Bandwidth Memory (HBM3) and eliminating kernel launch delays8.  
The NAFNet architecture is structured without dynamic shape breaks or conditional control flows, making it fully compatible with fullgraph=True compilation8. Compiling with mode="max-autotune-no-cudagraphs" triggers Triton autotuning, selecting optimal kernel tile dimensions, block sizes, and memory layouts specifically for the H100 compute architecture8. The compilation strategy employs explicit operator fusion configurations:

* Setting conv\_1x1\_as\_mm \= True converts ![][image10] spatial convolutions into dense Matrix Multiplication (GEMM) calls, mapping directly to H100 Tensor Cores to maximize TFLOPS utilization8.  
* Enabling coordinate\_descent\_tuning \= True searches the compiler layout space for optimal kernel memory access strides8.  
* Enabling epilogue\_fusion \= True fuses post-convolution activation and scaling steps directly into the output write phase of preceding GEMM kernels8.

Kernel fusion eliminates intermediate memory write-backs to HBM3 high-bandwidth memory, keeping activation tensors within local SRAM L1/L2 caches8.

### **Precision Calibration: BFloat16 and Tensor Core Optimization**

The NVIDIA H100 GPU features Transformer Engine hardware and 4th-generation Tensor Cores optimized for bfloat16 and fp8 precision arithmetic8. Running inference under torch.cuda.amp.autocast(dtype=torch.bfloat16) doubles memory throughput while cutting tensor memory footprints in half compared to standard float328.  
Unlike standard float16, which has a narrow dynamic range (![][image71] exponent bits) prone to underflow/overflow during unclipped speckle intensity processing, bfloat16 maintains an identical dynamic exponent range (![][image72] exponent bits) to float328. PyTorch Automatic Mixed Precision (AMP) automatically keeps numerically sensitive layers—such as LayerNormalization, log-transformations, and soft-clipping scaling—in float32 while executing high-FLOP convolutions in bfloat1622.

| Precision & Compilation Configuration | Dynamic Exponent Bits | H100 Compute Performance | Relative Inference Latency | Memory Footprint | Metric Preservation Fidelity |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **FP32 Eager Baseline** | 8 bits | \~60 TFLOPS | ![][image73] (Baseline) | ![][image73] | Full Baseline Precision22 |
| **FP16 Autocast (Eager)** | 5 bits | \~1000 TFLOPS | ![][image74] Speedup | ![][image75] | Underflow risk in speckle transformation8 |
| **BFloat16 Autocast (Eager)** | 8 bits | \~1000 TFLOPS | ![][image74] Speedup | ![][image75] | Bit-equivalent to FP3222 |
| **BF16 \+ torch.compile("default")** | 8 bits | \~1000 TFLOPS | ![][image76] Speedup | ![][image75] | Exact preservation22 |
| **BF16 \+ torch.compile("max-autotune")** | 8 bits | \~1000 TFLOPS | ![][image77] **Speedup** | **![][image75]** | Exact preservation22 |

### **Memory Transfers and Execution Stream Synchronization**

CUDA Graph execution (torch.cuda.make\_graphed\_callables) captures static sequence execution graphs during initial warmup passes, consolidating hundreds of discrete kernel launches into a single operation call submitted directly to the GPU hardware queue8. This reduces CPU launch overheads to near-zero levels (![][image78] per batch), maximizing GPU utilization even at small batch sizes8.  
To prevent hardware stalls during Host-to-Device (H2D) and Device-to-Host (D2H) memory transfers, operations are split across asynchronous CUDA streams (torch.cuda.Stream()). Asynchronous data transfers overlap memory copies over the PCIe bus with active Tensor Core compute cycles26.

## **End-to-End Computational Pipeline and Asynchronous Input-Output Optimization**

### **High-Throughput Image Decoding and Memory Pinning**

End-to-end evaluation runtime benchmarks include total execution time: script execution, model setup, disk I/O, GPU compute, and writing final predictions to storage. In high-performance evaluation environments on PCIe Gen5 storage, traditional CPU image reading (e.g., standard OpenCV cv2.imread or PIL Image.open) creates severe bottlenecks8. Single-threaded image decoding consumes substantial CPU time, leaving the H100 GPU idle.  
To maximize throughput, standard image reading libraries are replaced with nvJPEG (NVIDIA CUDA Accelerated JPEG Decoder) or multi-threaded C++ binding decoders such as PyTurboJPEG (libjpeg-turbo). nvJPEG decodes compressed image streams directly into CUDA GPU memory tensors, bypassing host CPU RAM allocation.  
When decoding on the CPU using PyTurboJPEG, host memory allocations must be locked into physical RAM using page-locked memory (pin\_memory=True). Pinned host memory enables direct memory access (DMA) transfers across the PCIe bus, maximizing H2D bandwidth without intermediate CPU buffering. Data ingestion uses non\_blocking=True flags during tensor movement to achieve true asynchronous transfer execution.

### **Parallel Micro-Batching and GPU Memory Footprint Management**

Given input resolution constraints (![][image2] or ![][image3] upsampled to ![][image1] or ![][image2]), single-image inference fails to utilize the parallel compute capacity of the H100 GPU23. Processing images in dynamic micro-batches maximizes Tensor Core occupancy23.  
Optimal batch sizes are selected to balance spatial memory requirements against Tensor Core tile utilization. For ![][image17] upsampling, a micro-batch size of ![][image79] or ![][image80] fully occupies H100 Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs) while operating comfortably within the 80GB HBM3 VRAM ceiling8.

### **Asynchronous Thread-Pool Disk Serialization**

Writing high-resolution (![][image1]) output images back to disk creates a disk I/O bottleneck if executed synchronously on the main GPU control thread. Standard sequential file saving forces the GPU to pause processing while waiting for disk write acknowledgments.  
To decouple GPU tensor execution from storage latencies, an Asynchronous Thread-Pool I/O Pipeline is implemented:

* The primary execution thread manages GPU batch ingestion, model execution, and soft-clipping post-processing without blocking.  
* As completed batches finish execution on the GPU, output tensors are copied asynchronously across CUDA Stream 2 into page-locked host CPU memory buffers.  
* A background worker pool (concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor configured with 16 worker threads) pops byte arrays from host queues, applies PNG/TIFF format encoding, and writes output files to storage concurrently23.

This asynchronous structure ensures the H100 GPU operates at 100% compute capacity throughout the evaluation run, completely hiding disk writing latency behind active neural network execution.

### **End-to-End System Execution Strategy**

The final deployment solution integrates all optimized stages into a continuous, high-throughput processing pipeline:

> 1. **Parallel Data Ingestion**: Raw degraded images are read from storage via multi-threaded PyTurboJPEG worker processes and staged into page-locked (pinned) host CPU memory buffers.  
> 2. **Asynchronous Memory Transfer**: Batched image arrays (![][image80]) are transferred to GPU VRAM across CUDA Stream 1 using non-blocking Direct Memory Access (non\_blocking=True).  
> 3. **Variance-Stabilizing Pre-Processing**: Input tensors are maintained in unclipped 32-bit floating-point format (float32), undergoing a logarithmic transformation (![][image84]) to convert multiplicative speckle noise into additive quasi-Gaussian noise3.  
> 4. **Compiled Model Inference**: The input batch passes through a fused, torch.compile-optimized NAFNet backbone executing under bfloat16 Automatic Mixed Precision8. Spatial upsampling (![][image85] or ![][image86]) is performed at the final layer via sub-pixel convolution13.  
> 5. **Parametric Dynamic Range Calibration**: Output feature maps pass through a parametric soft-clipping layer (![][image87]) to smoothly map restored pixel intensities back into the ground-truth interval ![][image25] without zeroing gradients.  
> 6. **Asynchronous Serialization**: Restored high-resolution image batches are copied to host CPU memory across CUDA Stream 2, where a 16-worker background thread pool encodes and writes target PNG/TIFF files to disk concurrently23.

## **Conclusions and Actionable Implementation Summary**

Restoring signal-degraded, downsampled images containing multiplicative speckle and additive Gaussian noise requires a balanced co-design of deep neural architecture, mathematical loss formulation, dynamic range handling, and hardware-level inference optimization:

* **Architectural Selection**: Employ a modified U-shaped **Nonlinear Activation-Free Network (NAFNet)** featuring **Sub-Pixel Convolution (PixelShuffle)** upsampling heads11. Replacing standard nonlinearities with **SimpleGate** activations and **Simplified Channel Attention (SCA)** delivers high restoration fidelity while minimizing computational complexity and memory access latency11.  
* **Pre-Processing & Calibration**: Ingest raw, unclipped 32-bit floating-point tensors to preserve out-of-bounds intensity data caused by speckle noise. Apply a **Logarithmic Variance Stabilizing Transformation** during feature extraction, paired with **Parametric Soft-Clipping** at the network output layer to smoothly constrain final pixel values to ![][image25]3.  
* **Loss Function Formulation**: Train using a compound multi-objective objective combining **Charbonnier Loss** (pixel fidelity / PSNR), **MS-SSIM Loss** (structural fidelity / SSIM), **LPIPS Loss** (perceptual micro-textures), and **Sobel Gradient Loss** (edge sharpness)4. Balance dynamic loss components using Multi-Objective Optimization to maximize scores across all target metrics19.  
* **Hardware Acceleration**: Execute inference under **PyTorch AMP bfloat16** precision to maximize H100 Tensor Core throughput while avoiding half-precision numerical underflow8. Compile the execution graph via torch.compile(mode="max-autotune-no-cudagraphs") to generate fused Triton kernels and eliminate CUDA launch overheads8.  
* **I/O Pipeline Engineering**: Eliminate disk access bottlenecks by combining **PyTurboJPEG** CPU decoding, **pinned host memory transfers**, micro-batching (![][image80]), and a 16-worker **Asynchronous Thread-Pool** serialization pipeline to completely decouple disk writing from GPU computation cycles8.
